blocks.text: TTP is a rare, life-threatening **thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA)**. Its defining paradox is **widespread small-vessel thrombosis together with a low platelet count**, a pairing it shares with DIC and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. The root problem is a lack of functional **ADAMTS-13**, the protease that trims von Willebrand factor (vWF). It can strike any organ, responds well to treatment, and is usually fatal if missed.

blocks.title: The classic pentad (only a minority have all five)
items: **Thrombocytopenia**
**Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA)** with red cell fragments
**Neurological** disturbance
**Fever**
**Renal impairment**

blocks.title: Forms of TTP and their triggers
rows: Most sporadic cases show true enzyme deficiency with an inhibitor
Thienopyridines (**ticlopidine, clopidogrel**), **ciclosporin**, quinidine; stepup6 also lists quinine, chemotherapy and immunosuppressants
**Pregnancy and the post-partum period**, oral contraceptives
**SLE**, **HIV**, other infections, **malignancy**; Davidson also lists Shiga toxins

blocks.text: TTP affects roughly **1 in 750 000 people per year**. Kumar notes that **young adults** are the group most often affected, and First Aid contrasts TTP (mainly adults) with HUS (mainly children).
Up to **one-quarter** of TTP/HUS cases arise **during pregnancy or after delivery**, so TTP belongs in the differential of low platelets in pregnancy.
In **HIV**, a TTP-like illness with severe thrombocytopenia and MAHA can occur; it carries a **better prognosis and fewer relapses** than classical TTP.

Classic exam trigger: a patient recently started on **clopidogrel or ticlopidine** who develops low platelets, fragmented red cells and confusion. Think **drug-associated TTP**, and remember the precipitating drug must be stopped.
Secondary TTP (pregnancy, drugs, SLE, infection) may show **variable ADAMTS-13 activity** and may **lack detectable antibodies**, unlike typical idiopathic acquired TTP.

**ADAMTS-13**, a metalloproteinase that regulates vWF, normally cuts **ultra-large vWF multimers** into normal-sized units. When the enzyme is missing or blocked, the huge multimers stay anchored to the endothelium and **grab and cross-link platelets**, building **platelet-rich microthrombi** in arterioles and capillaries. The organs hit hardest are the **brain and kidneys**, but any organ can be involved.

blocks.title: What the microthrombi do
items: **Consume platelets** → profound thrombocytopenia
**Shear red cells** passing through narrowed vessels → fragments (**schistocytes**) and intravascular haemolysis (MAHA)
**Occlude small vessels** → ischaemic end-organ damage (fluctuating neurology, kidney injury)

blocks.alt: Flow chart: low ADAMTS-13 activity leads to persistent ultra-large vWF multimers, then platelet-rich microthrombi, which cause platelet consumption, red cell shearing (MAHA) and small-vessel occlusion.

blocks.text: Because the thrombi form on vWF and platelets rather than through runaway activation of the clotting cascade, **clotting factors and fibrinogen are not used up**. PT, APTT and fibrinogen therefore stay normal, unlike **DIC**, where factors (notably V and VIII) and fibrinogen are consumed.

blocks.title: Histology
items: Tissue biopsy in a TMA shows **arterioles plugged with platelet hyaline thrombi**
The same picture of glomerular microthrombi is seen in HUS renal biopsies

blocks.text: Platelets are low **because they are being used up**, not because the marrow fails: the marrow shows **increased megakaryocytes** in consumptive thrombocytopenia.
Transfused platelets are simply **fed into the microthrombi** and can worsen the thrombosis, which is why platelet transfusion is contraindicated.

blocks.title: The pentad: what you see and how often
rows: **Fluctuating, transient** — confusion, delirium, seizures, stroke or hemiplegia, drowsiness, visual loss

blocks.title: How to recognise it
items: Mnemonic **LMNOP**: Low platelets, MAHA, Neuro change, “Obsolete” kidneys, Pyrexia
First Aid: **suspect TTP when 3 of the 5** are present
The **full pentad occurs in only ~5%**; thrombocytopenia plus MAHA is the constant core

blocks.text: Against **HUS**, TTP more often involves the **brain**, while the **kidney is usually less prominent**. In pregnancy both cause MAHA, AKI and low platelets, but **neurological symptoms and fever point to TTP**.

blocks.title: Less obvious presentations listed by Davidson
items: **Seizures in pregnancy** (with eclampsia and cerebral venous thrombosis)
A haematological cause of **pyrexia of unknown origin**
A haematological **sepsis mimic** (alongside haemophagocytic syndrome and lymphoma)

blocks.text: Spontaneous bleeding from thrombocytopenia is unusual until platelets drop **below 20 × 10⁹/L**; **below 10 × 10⁹/L** retinal and intracranial bleeding become possible.
Do **not** wait for all five features. Waiting for fever or renal failure delays treatment of a disease that kills most untreated patients within days.

A TMA is diagnosed from **unexplained thrombocytopenia (often < 20 × 10⁹/L) plus MAHA**. The **blood film** is the single most useful first test for a low platelet count. **ADAMTS-13 activity** is the most accurate test for TTP itself.

blocks.title: Expected results in TTP
rows: **LDH markedly raised**, unconjugated bilirubin up, **haptoglobin very low**, reticulocytes often up
Intravascular haemolysis (LDH also from tissue ischaemia)
Reduced in TTP but normal in HUS and other TMAs

blocks.title: Using the tests
items: Measure **ADAMTS-13 activity whenever TTP or HUS is suspected**
The **PLASMIC score** helps separate TTP from other TMAs
Follow treatment with **serial platelet counts and LDH**

blocks.note: Panel E: red cell fragments of intravascular haemolysis, as in MAHA (HUS, TTP) and DIC.
Peripheral film with arrowed schistocytes (MAHA or mechanical valve haemolysis).

blocks.text: Normal **PT and APTT** in a patient with low platelets and fragments is the classic clue that this is TTP/HUS rather than DIC, because TTP does not consume clotting factors.
The sources phrase the ADAMTS-13 result differently: Davidson gives a cut-off of **< 10%**, Kumar simply says “reduced”, and the quick sources give no number. Follow Davidson for the threshold.

blocks.title: TTP and its mimics
rows: Bloody diarrhoea (E. coli O157:H7), mostly children, renal failure dominant
Family history, no diarrhoea; complement factor mutations
Quinine (with fever), calcineurin or VEGF-A inhibitors
Very high BP, retinopathy with papilloedema
Breast, prostate, lung, pancreas, GI tumours; skin features of scleroderma
Treat tumour; ACE inhibitor in scleroderma

blocks.text: Memory aid: **HUS = MAHA + low platelets + renal failure**; **TTP ≈ HUS + fever + altered mental state**. Kidney dominates HUS, brain dominates TTP.

blocks.title: Other causes of red cell fragments
items: Mechanical heart valves
March haemoglobinuria
Severe burns
Disseminated carcinoma, malignant or pregnancy-induced hypertension

blocks.title: Low platelets in pregnancy
items: **Gestational thrombocytopenia** — commonest, late in pregnancy, harmless, resolves after delivery
ITP
SLE
HELLP
HUS and **TTP**

blocks.text: **ITP** gives isolated immune destruction of platelets with **no haemolysis** and normal or increased marrow megakaryocytes; it is often a diagnosis of exclusion. Step-Up groups TTP with DIC, HUS and HIT type 1 as **non-immune** destructive causes, versus immune causes such as ITP, SLE, HIT type 2 and HIV.

blocks.note: Haemolysis classification: TTP, HUS and DIC sit with the acquired, mechanical (microangiopathic) causes.
Renal light microscopy in HUS: arrow marks glomerular microthrombi of a thrombotic microangiopathy.

blocks.text: First Aid describes HUS and TTP as one spectrum caused by ADAMTS-13 deficiency. The major texts disagree: Davidson attributes HUS to **Shiga toxin or complement abnormalities** and uses a **low ADAMTS-13 (< 10%)** to separate TTP from HUS, and Kumar states that **ADAMTS-13 activity is normal in HUS**. Follow Davidson.

Davidson lists Shiga toxins among TTP associations, but a Shiga-toxin TMA with bloody diarrhoea and dominant renal failure is **HUS**, which is managed **supportively** rather than with plasma exchange.

TTP is a **haematological emergency**. **Emergency plasma exchange** is the cornerstone and best first treatment. Start it as soon as the diagnosis is made, and stop once the platelet count has recovered.

blocks.title: Treatment options
rows: Removes the anti-ADAMTS-13 antibody and supplies fresh ADAMTS-13
FFP if plasma exchange is delayed
Pulsed IV methylprednisolone in the acute phase
Increasingly first-line (Kumar); used when ADAMTS-13 is confirmed low or for relapse prevention
Anti-vWF single-variable-domain immunoglobulin; blocks vWF binding to platelet glycoprotein Ib
Faster platelet recovery and fewer recurrences
Listed by Davidson as having a role
Withdraw any causative drug in secondary TTP

blocks.text: **Platelet transfusion is contraindicated** in TTP, even with very low counts. The transfused platelets fuel more microthrombi.

blocks.title: Prognosis
items: Untreated: about **90% mortality within the first 10 days**
Even with proper treatment: **20–30% mortality at 6 months**
Relapse is common, often linked to **persistently absent ADAMTS-13**
The HIV-associated TTP-like illness has a better outlook

blocks.text: **In pregnancy**, TTP is treated with plasma exchange and FFP, sometimes adding glucocorticoids or rituximab; platelet transfusion is again avoided.
Contrast the mimics: **Shiga-toxin HUS** is managed supportively, **complement-mediated HUS** with plasma exchange and **eculizumab**, and **DIC** by treating its cause.

Sources differ on rituximab: Kumar and kcEssentials give it upfront with steroids, Step-Up gives it once ADAMTS-13 is confirmed low, and Pocket Medicine frames it as relapse prevention. Davidson simply lists it as having a role.

cards.back: Thrombocytopenia, MAHA, neurological change, fever, renal impairment (few patients have all five)

cards.front: Antiplatelet drugs classically linked to TTP?

cards.back: Cleaves ultra-large vWF multimers into normal-sized units

cards.front: Why are PT and APTT normal in TTP?
cards.back: Thrombi are platelet–vWF based; clotting factors and fibrinogen are not consumed

cards.front: How often is the full TTP pentad present?
cards.back: Only ~5%; thrombocytopenia + MAHA are present in essentially all

cards.front: TTP vs HUS: which organ dominates each?
cards.back: TTP: brain (neurological features). HUS: kidney (renal failure)
LDH markedly raised, unconjugated bilirubin up, haptoglobin very low, schistocytes, DAT negative
< 10%; activity is normal in HUS and other TMAs

cards.front: Markers to follow TTP during treatment?
Lab clue for DIC rather than TTP?
cards.back: Prolonged PT/APTT, low fibrinogen, raised D-dimer

cards.front: First-line treatment of TTP and its rationale?
cards.back: Emergency plasma exchange: removes the antibody and replaces ADAMTS-13
Anti-vWF agent blocking vWF–glycoprotein Ib binding; faster platelet recovery, fewer recurrences
Untreated ~90% within 10 days; treated 20–30% at 6 months

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man had a coronary stent placed 3 weeks ago and was started on a new antiplatelet agent. He now has episodes of confusion and widespread petechiae. Hb 84 g/L, platelets 14 × 10⁹/L, fragmented red cells on the film, PT and APTT normal.
questions.leadIn: Which of his medicines is most likely to have triggered this illness?
questions.explanation: Low platelets, MAHA and fluctuating neurology after starting a **thienopyridine** suggest **drug-associated TTP**. Clopidogrel and ticlopidine are the classic culprits, and the drug must be stopped.
whyNot: Statins are not among the drugs the sources link to TTP (thienopyridines, ciclosporin, quinidine).
Beta-blockers are not among the drugs the sources link to TTP.
ACE inhibitors are not among the drugs the sources link to TTP.
Nitrates are not among the drugs the sources link to TTP.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has her first episode of TTP. She takes no medicines, is not pregnant and has no family history. ADAMTS-13 activity is 4% with an inhibitor detected.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely underlying mechanism?
options: Shiga toxin binding to renal endothelium
Inherited mutation of complement factor H
Systemic activation of coagulation with factor consumption
questions.explanation: Most acquired, sporadic TTP is an **autoimmune** disease: IgG autoantibodies block ADAMTS-13, so ultra-large vWF multimers persist. A detectable inhibitor fits this.
whyNot: Shiga toxin causes diarrhoea-associated HUS, with normal ADAMTS-13.
Complement factor H mutations cause atypical HUS, with normal ADAMTS-13.
PF4–heparin antibodies cause HIT, which needs heparin exposure.
Coagulation activation with factor consumption is DIC, where PT/APTT are prolonged.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with TTP has a platelet count of 9 × 10⁹/L. A student asks why the count is so low.
questions.leadIn: What is the main reason for the thrombocytopenia?
options: Platelets consumed in microthrombi built on ultra-large vWF multimers
Pooling of platelets in an enlarged spleen
Antibody-coated platelets cleared by splenic macrophages
questions.explanation: TTP is a **consumptive** thrombocytopenia: persistent ultra-large vWF multimers capture platelets into microthrombi, using them up. The marrow typically has plenty of megakaryocytes.
whyNot: Marrow failure causes reduced production; consumptive causes show increased megakaryocytes.
Hypersplenism is mechanical pooling, not TTP.
Dilution follows massive transfusion or fluids, not TTP.
Antibody-mediated platelet clearance describes ITP.

questions.stem: In TTP, a deficient protease allows very large multimers of an adhesive plasma protein to persist on the endothelium.
questions.leadIn: Which enzyme normally cleaves these multimers?
questions.explanation: **ADAMTS-13** cuts ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers into normal-sized units. Lack of it is the central defect in TTP.
whyNot: Plasmin breaks down fibrin, not vWF multimers.
Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin.
Activated protein C inactivates factors Va and VIIIa.
Antithrombin inhibits thrombin and factor Xa.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman is admitted with suspected TTP. The registrar reminds the team that the full pentad is uncommon.
questions.leadIn: Which pair of features is present in essentially every patient with TTP?
questions.explanation: Thrombocytopenia and MAHA are present in about **100%**. Neurological change occurs in ~65%, renal failure ~50% and fever only ~25%; the full pentad occurs in about 5%.
whyNot: Fever (~25%) and renal failure (~50%) are often absent.
Neurology (~65%) and fever (~25%) are not constant.
Renal failure is present in only about half.
Fever is the least consistent pentad feature.

questions.stem: Two adults present with microangiopathic haemolysis and thrombocytopenia. One has fluctuating confusion and the other has severe oliguric kidney injury.
questions.leadIn: Which organ is characteristically more involved in TTP than in HUS?
questions.explanation: Davidson notes that the **brain** is more often affected in TTP, while **kidney** involvement is usually less prominent than in HUS.
whyNot: Kidney involvement dominates HUS, and is usually milder in TTP.
Abnormal liver tests point towards HELLP rather than TTP.
Lung involvement is not the distinguishing feature.
Bloody diarrhoea points to Shiga-toxin HUS.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man has confusion, purpura, Hb 79 g/L and platelets 12 × 10⁹/L.
questions.leadIn: Which set of results best fits TTP?
options: High LDH, low haptoglobin, normal PT and fibrinogen, negative DAT
High LDH, low haptoglobin, prolonged PT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer
Normal LDH, normal haptoglobin, isolated low platelets, normal film
High LDH, low haptoglobin, positive DAT, spherocytes on film
Normal LDH, raised MCV, hypersegmented neutrophils, normal haptoglobin
questions.explanation: TTP gives **intravascular mechanical haemolysis** (high LDH, low haptoglobin, DAT negative) with a **normal coagulation screen**, because clotting factors are not consumed.
whyNot: Prolonged PT, low fibrinogen and high D-dimer indicate DIC.
An isolated low platelet count without haemolysis suggests ITP.
A positive DAT with spherocytes suggests autoimmune haemolysis.
There are no markers of haemolysis, so this is not a TMA picture.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman has thrombocytopenia, schistocytes, raised LDH and transient dysphasia. The team wants to confirm the diagnosis.
questions.leadIn: Which test is the most accurate for confirming TTP?
options: Stool culture for E. coli O157:H7
questions.explanation: **ADAMTS-13 activity** is the most accurate test. It is low in TTP (< 10% in Davidson) but normal in HUS and other TMAs.
whyNot: The DAT detects immune haemolysis and is negative in TTP.
D-dimer helps identify DIC.
Stool culture supports Shiga-toxin HUS.
Marrow shows only increased megakaryocytes in consumptive causes and is not diagnostic.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 31 weeks of pregnancy has a generalised seizure. Temperature 38.4 °C, BP 124/78 mmHg. Platelets 18 × 10⁹/L, Hb 86 g/L, fragments on the film, LDH very high. LFTs, PT and APTT are normal; urine has no protein.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: MAHA plus low platelets with **fever and neurological features**, a **normal BP**, normal LFTs and no proteinuria point to **TTP**, which is a recognised cause of seizures in pregnancy.
whyNot: Eclampsia follows pre-eclampsia, with hypertension and proteinuria.
HELLP occurs late in pregnancy with abnormal LFTs.
Gestational thrombocytopenia is mild and has no haemolysis.
ITP does not cause MAHA, fever or seizures.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man is in septic shock from cholangitis. He is oozing from cannula sites. Platelets 32 × 10⁹/L, occasional fragments on the film, PT and APTT prolonged, fibrinogen 0.7 g/L, D-dimer very high.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of his thrombocytopenia?
questions.explanation: Sepsis with bleeding and a **consumptive coagulopathy** (long PT/APTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer) is **DIC**. In TTP the clotting screen is normal.
whyNot: TTP has a normal PT, APTT and fibrinogen.
HUS follows bloody diarrhoea and has normal clotting tests.
ITP does not prolong clotting times or lower fibrinogen.
HIT needs heparin exposure and does not cause this coagulopathy.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman has confirmed TTP with platelets 10 × 10⁹/L and fluctuating confusion.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate first treatment?
questions.explanation: **Emergency plasma exchange** removes the anti-ADAMTS-13 antibody and supplies the enzyme. It is the cornerstone of treatment and should start as soon as the diagnosis is made.
whyNot: Platelet transfusion is contraindicated: it fuels microthrombosis.
IVIG is used in ITP, not as TTP first-line therapy.
Splenectomy is a second-line ITP treatment.
Supportive care alone leaves untreated TTP with ~90% early mortality.

questions.stem: A junior doctor plans treatment for a man with TTP whose platelet count is 7 × 10⁹/L.
questions.leadIn: Which intervention is contraindicated?
questions.explanation: **Platelet concentrates are contraindicated** in TTP: the extra platelets feed the microthrombi and can worsen the illness.
whyNot: Plasma exchange is the mainstay of treatment.
Pulsed methylprednisolone is given in the acute phase.
Rituximab is increasingly part of primary treatment.
Caplacizumab speeds platelet recovery and reduces recurrence.

questions.stem: A woman with acquired TTP is started on plasma exchange and steroids. The haematologist adds a drug that targets von Willebrand factor.
questions.leadIn: What is the mechanism of this added drug (caplacizumab)?
options: Blocks vWF binding to platelet glycoprotein Ib
Blocks terminal complement activation at C5
questions.explanation: Caplacizumab is an anti-vWF single-variable-domain immunoglobulin that **stops vWF interacting with platelet glycoprotein Ib**, giving faster platelet recovery and fewer recurrences.
whyNot: This is eculizumab, used in complement-mediated HUS.
Thrombopoietin receptor agonists (e.g. eltrombopag) are used in refractory ITP.
This describes aspirin.
Antithrombin-dependent inhibition of Xa describes heparins and fondaparinux.

questions.stem: A medical student asks how dangerous TTP is if it is not treated.
questions.leadIn: What is the approximate mortality of untreated TTP within the first 10 days?
questions.explanation: Davidson quotes about **90% mortality in the first 10 days** without treatment; with appropriate therapy mortality is still 20–30% at 6 months.
whyNot: Too low for untreated TTP.
This is the 6-month mortality despite treatment.
Far below the untreated figure.
Far below the untreated figure.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy had bloody diarrhoea 5 days after eating an undercooked burger at a barbecue. He is now passing little urine. Creatinine is markedly raised, platelets 45 × 10⁹/L, fragments on the film, PT and APTT normal. He is alert and orientated.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A child with **bloody diarrhoea**, dominant **renal failure**, MAHA and no neurological features has **Shiga-toxin (E. coli O157:H7) HUS**, managed supportively.
whyNot: TTP usually affects adults and has prominent neurology with milder renal involvement.
Atypical HUS lacks preceding bloody diarrhoea and often has a family history.
DIC prolongs PT and APTT.
ITP causes no haemolysis or kidney injury.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has MAHA, platelets 60 × 10⁹/L and acute kidney injury without diarrhoea. His mother and uncle had similar episodes. ADAMTS-13 activity is 70%.
questions.leadIn: Which targeted treatment is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Normal ADAMTS-13, a **family history** and no diarrhoea suggest **complement-mediated (atypical) HUS**. Treatment is plasma exchange with **eculizumab**, an anti-C5 antibody.
whyNot: Caplacizumab targets vWF and is used in TTP, which is excluded by a normal ADAMTS-13.
Eltrombopag is used in refractory ITP.
Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic and does not block complement, the driver of this illness.
Heparin is not used to treat atypical HUS.

questions.stem: A woman is receiving daily plasma exchange for TTP. The team needs to judge whether the disease is settling.
questions.leadIn: Which pair of tests is best for following disease activity?
questions.explanation: Kumar recommends following **serial platelet counts and LDH**. Recovery of the platelet count also tells you when plasma exchange can stop.
whyNot: These track DIC, not TTP activity.
Inflammatory markers do not reflect microvascular thrombosis.
Iron studies are irrelevant here.
Haematinics are not activity markers.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has a platelet count of 22 × 10⁹/L on a routine test. The cause is unclear.
questions.leadIn: Which single investigation is the most useful first step?
questions.explanation: Davidson calls the **blood film** the single most useful initial test for thrombocytopenia: it checks for clumping, fragments and other abnormal cells.
whyNot: Marrow is a later test, used to show megakaryocytes or infiltration.
Platelet antibodies are not needed to diagnose ITP.
ADAMTS-13 is sent once a TMA picture is found.
A clotting screen helps identify DIC but is not the first step for low platelets.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman has thrombocytopenia, MAHA and a raised creatinine. The team is trying to separate TTP from HUS.
questions.leadIn: Which ADAMTS-13 activity result, according to Davidson, favours TTP?
questions.explanation: Davidson states that an ADAMTS-13 activity **below 10%** helps distinguish TTP from HUS. Activity is normal in HUS and other TMAs.
whyNot: Not low enough to indicate TTP.
Within the range seen in HUS and other TMAs.
A normal level argues against TTP.
A high-normal level argues against TTP.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman has been taking quinine for night cramps. She develops fever, acute kidney injury, fragmented red cells and platelets 40 × 10⁹/L. PT and APTT are normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the key step in management?
questions.explanation: Quinine is a cause of **drug-induced TMA** (often with fever). Davidson lists **stopping the offending drug** as the management.
whyNot: Platelet transfusion is avoided in TMAs such as TTP/HUS.
Heparin is not a treatment for drug-induced TMA.
Splenectomy is an ITP treatment.
IVIG treats immune platelet destruction, not a drug TMA.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman has 2 days of confusion and word-finding difficulty that come and go. She has petechiae and a temperature of 38.2 °C. Hb 78 g/L, platelets 11 × 10⁹/L, fragmented red cells on the film. LDH 1850 U/L, unconjugated bilirubin raised, haptoglobin undetectable. PT, APTT and fibrinogen are normal. DAT negative. Creatinine 140 µmol/L.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Step 1: low platelets plus **fragments, high LDH and absent haptoglobin** = microangiopathic haemolysis, so this is a TMA. Step 2: **normal PT, APTT and fibrinogen** exclude DIC. Step 3: a **negative DAT** excludes immune haemolysis. Step 4: **fluctuating neurology and fever** with only mild renal impairment point to **TTP** rather than HUS. Next: send ADAMTS-13 and start plasma exchange urgently.
whyNot: DIC would prolong PT/APTT and lower fibrinogen.
ITP causes no haemolysis, fever or neurology.
Warm AIHA gives a positive DAT and spherocytes, with no thrombocytopenia from consumption.
Shiga-toxin HUS follows bloody diarrhoea, with renal failure dominant and no neurology.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man has newly diagnosed TTP with platelets 9 × 10⁹/L and gum bleeding. An ADAMTS-13 result is expected in 3 days. The night team asks what to do first.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Transfuse platelets to stop the bleeding
Wait for the ADAMTS-13 result before treating
questions.explanation: Step 1: TTP is a **haematological emergency**: untreated mortality is ~90% in 10 days. Step 2: **early plasma exchange is crucial**, so start it once the clinical and lab picture fits, not after the confirmatory assay. Step 3: resist the instinct to give platelets despite the very low count: **platelet transfusion is contraindicated** because it fuels thrombosis. Add steroids, and consider rituximab and caplacizumab.
whyNot: Platelets are contraindicated in TTP.
Delay is dangerous; early plasma exchange is crucial.
IVIG is an ITP treatment.
Supportive care alone is inadequate.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 37 weeks of pregnancy is well. Routine bloods show platelets 112 × 10⁹/L, a normal Hb, a normal film and normal LFTs. BP is 118/72 mmHg.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of her low platelets?
questions.explanation: Step 1: work through the pregnancy causes (gestational, ITP, SLE, HELLP, HUS, TTP). Step 2: there is **no haemolysis** (normal Hb and film), which excludes TTP and HUS. Step 3: normal BP and LFTs exclude HELLP. Step 4: a mild fall late in pregnancy in a well woman is **gestational thrombocytopenia**, the commonest and a benign cause.
whyNot: TTP needs MAHA, and usually much lower platelets.
HELLP has haemolysis, abnormal LFTs and hypertension.
ITP is possible but is less common than gestational thrombocytopenia in this setting.
HUS causes MAHA and AKI.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl has had several episodes of thrombocytopenia with fragmented red cells since infancy. Her ADAMTS-13 activity is undetectable and no inhibitor is found. Her brother is similarly affected.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Inherited ADAMTS-13 deficiency without an inhibitor is congenital TTP, called **Upshaw–Schulman syndrome**.
whyNot: Bernard–Soulier is a platelet adhesion defect (missing GPIb complex), without haemolysis.
Glanzmann’s is a GPIIb/IIIa aggregation defect without thrombocytopenia from consumption.
Wiskott–Aldrich gives small platelets, not MAHA.
May–Hegglin is an inherited macrothrombocytopathy, not a TMA.

questions.stem: A man with TTP is waiting for plasma exchange, which will take some hours to arrange.
questions.leadIn: Which blood product contains ADAMTS-13 and can be given in the meantime?
questions.explanation: Solvent-detergent FFP (and cryoprecipitate) contain **ADAMTS-13**. Pocket Medicine advises FFP if plasma exchange is delayed.
whyNot: Platelets are contraindicated in TTP.
Red cells are not a source of ADAMTS-13; the sources name only plasma products (SD-FFP, cryoprecipitate).
Albumin is not listed as a source of ADAMTS-13; only SD-FFP and cryoprecipitate are.
PCC is used to reverse warfarin and is not listed as a source of ADAMTS-13.

questions.stem: A student is learning the TTP pentad and its frequencies.
questions.leadIn: Which pentad feature is present least often?
questions.explanation: Fever occurs in only about **25%** of patients, against ~100% for low platelets and MAHA, ~65% for neurological change and ~50% for renal failure.
whyNot: Present in essentially all patients.
Present in essentially all patients.
Present in about two-thirds.
Present in about half.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman was treated for acquired TTP a year ago and is now in clinical remission with a normal platelet count.
questions.leadIn: Which finding is most associated with a risk of relapse?
options: Reticulocyte count within the reference range
questions.explanation: Kumar notes that recurrent and relapsing TTP is often linked to a **persistent lack of ADAMTS-13**. Rituximab is used to help prevent relapse.
whyNot: A normal LDH indicates no active haemolysis.
A normal haptoglobin indicates no active haemolysis.
PT is normal in TTP, active or not.
A normal reticulocyte count reflects no ongoing haemolysis.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman has 4 days of petechiae and nosebleeds. Platelets 8 × 10⁹/L, Hb 134 g/L, the film shows no fragments and LDH is normal. She is otherwise well and afebrile.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Isolated severe thrombocytopenia with **no haemolysis** (normal Hb, no fragments, normal LDH) in a well young woman suggests **ITP**, often a diagnosis of exclusion.
whyNot: TTP needs MAHA with fragments and a raised LDH.
DIC occurs in sick patients with abnormal clotting tests.
HUS needs MAHA and AKI.
Aplastic anaemia lowers all cell lines, so Hb would be low too.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man presents with headache and blurred vision. BP 238/142 mmHg, papilloedema on fundoscopy, creatinine rising, Hb 95 g/L, platelets 70 × 10⁹/L and fragments on the film. PT and APTT are normal. He is alert and orientated.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of the microangiopathy?
questions.explanation: In Davidson’s TMA table, **very high BP with hypertensive retinopathy and papilloedema** points to malignant hypertension, treated by controlling BP.
whyNot: TTP has prominent neurology and very low platelets; severe hypertension with papilloedema points elsewhere.
There is no bloody diarrhoea.
Clotting tests are normal.
There is no family history, and the hypertensive retinopathy explains the picture.

questions.theme: Causes of red cell fragmentation and low platelets
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the best-fitting diagnosis from the options. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has 3 days of intermittent confusion and fever. Platelets 12 × 10⁹/L, fragments on the film, PT and APTT normal, ADAMTS-13 activity 3% with an inhibitor present.
items.explanation: Fever, fluctuating neurology and MAHA with **very low ADAMTS-13 plus an inhibitor** = acquired autoimmune TTP.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man with a metallic aortic valve replacement has fatigue. Hb 96 g/L, fragments on the film, raised LDH, low haptoglobin, platelets 210 × 10⁹/L.
items.explanation: Fragments and intravascular haemolysis with a **normal platelet count** in a patient with a prosthetic valve suggest mechanical valve haemolysis, not a TMA.

items.stem: A woman at 34 weeks of pregnancy has right upper quadrant pain. BP 162/104 mmHg, ALT 410 U/L, platelets 58 × 10⁹/L, fragments on the film.
items.explanation: Third trimester, hypertension and **abnormal LFTs** with haemolysis and low platelets = HELLP, which resolves with delivery.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man is in septic shock from an abdominal source and is bleeding from line sites. Platelets 30 × 10⁹/L, fragments present, PT prolonged, fibrinogen 0.6 g/L.
items.explanation: Two steps: the film and platelets suggest a TMA, but the **prolonged PT and low fibrinogen** in a septic, bleeding patient show coagulation consumption = DIC.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman is 5 days post-partum. She has a seizure, then remains confused. Temperature 38.3 °C, BP 126/80 mmHg. Platelets 15 × 10⁹/L, fragments on the film, LDH very high, LFTs normal, PT and APTT normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Post-partum MAHA, thrombocytopenia, fever and seizures with normal BP, LFTs and clotting point to **TTP**. Treatment is **plasma exchange** (with FFP and sometimes steroids or rituximab); platelets are avoided.
whyNot: Magnesium treats eclampsia, which needs hypertension; BP is normal here.
Platelet transfusion should be avoided in TTP.
LMWH is for cerebral venous thrombosis, which does not explain MAHA.
IVIG is an ITP treatment.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman has MAHA, platelets 25 × 10⁹/L and a creatinine of 210 µmol/L. She has mild confusion but no diarrhoea.
questions.leadIn: Which result would most strongly support TTP over HUS?
options: Stool PCR positive for Shiga toxin
questions.explanation: A **very low ADAMTS-13 activity** (< 10%) separates TTP from HUS, in which ADAMTS-13 is normal.
whyNot: Low haptoglobin occurs in both TTP and HUS.
Complement mutations point to atypical HUS.
Shiga toxin points to diarrhoea-associated HUS.
Schistocytes are seen in both.

questions.stem: A pathologist examines tissue from a patient who died of untreated TTP.
questions.leadIn: What are the occluding microvascular thrombi mainly composed of?
options: Platelets bound to von Willebrand factor
Fibrin formed after consumption of clotting factors
questions.explanation: Ultra-large vWF multimers cross-link **platelets**, producing **platelet-rich (hyaline) thrombi** in arterioles and capillaries.
whyNot: Fibrin-rich thrombi with factor consumption describe DIC.
Cholesterol emboli follow arterial instrumentation.
Sickling causes vaso-occlusion in sickle cell disease.
Immune complex deposition is a vasculitis mechanism.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man with acquired TTP is receiving daily plasma exchange and methylprednisolone. The haematologist wants an agent that targets von Willebrand factor to speed platelet recovery and reduce recurrence.
questions.leadIn: Which drug fits this description?
questions.explanation: **Caplacizumab** blocks the vWF–glycoprotein Ib interaction, giving faster platelet recovery and fewer recurrences.
whyNot: Eculizumab blocks C5 and is used in complement-mediated HUS.
Eltrombopag is a thrombopoietin agonist used in ITP.
Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic and does not act on von Willebrand factor.
Heparin does not target the vWF–platelet interaction.

questions.stem: A patient has thrombocytopenia and red cell fragments on the blood film.
questions.leadIn: Which finding would most suggest DIC rather than TTP?
options: Prolonged PT and APTT with low fibrinogen
questions.explanation: DIC consumes clotting factors and fibrinogen, so **PT and APTT are prolonged and fibrinogen is low**. In TTP these are normal.
whyNot: LDH is high in both.
Fragments occur in both.
Haptoglobin is low in both.
Severe thrombocytopenia occurs in both.

ospe.identify: Panel E: red cell fragments (schistocytes) → intravascular, microangiopathic haemolysis, as in TTP, HUS or DIC
Arrowed fragmented red cells (schistocytes) → MAHA (TTP/HUS) or mechanical valve haemolysis; with low platelets and confusion, think TTP
Glomerulus with arrowed microthrombi → thrombotic microangiopathy (renal lesion typical of HUS; TTP is the main differential)
